documents.abstract: Boundary — Future Editions System is an integrated, future-oriented research and software development framework within the Recoverability-Constrained Systems (RCS) and Continuity Science corpus developed by Noelia Sanchez / Interval Studio Ltd. The system extends the established Boundary research architecture by introducing a reusable framework for generating, organizing, evaluating, validating, documenting and managing successive research and software editions while preserving the integrity, traceability and recoverability of earlier work. Rather than treating research publications as isolated or permanently closed artifacts, the framework establishes a structured relationship between finite formal systems and open-ended scientific and technological development. Its central objective is to enable continuous advancement without sacrificing evidence, safety, human autonomy, accountability or the capacity to recover from unsuccessful changes. Foundational Architecture The framework integrates finite successor-space mathematics, recoverability-constrained admissibility, recursive governance, distinction preservation, terminal closure, interdisciplinary interoperability and living-system continuity. Its nine-dimensional finite architecture comprises: Domain Object Transformation Evidence Failure Protection Interval Authority Outcome With nine defined categories per dimension, the reference model supports 387,420,489 mathematically indexable combinations (9⁹). These combinations are represented through deterministic indexing rather than requiring the physical storage or experimental validation of every combination. The framework also supports incremental generation of future research candidates, including new hypotheses, technical specifications, system architectures and possible applications. This open-ended capability does not represent a completed infinite enumeration or establish that every future discovery has already been identified. Executable Future-Edition System The accompanying software package provides an offline, Python-based foundation for generating candidate Boundary editions. Its capabilities include edition identification and numbering, finite combination indexing, provenance preservation, source-integrity verification, candidate-generation procedures, safety checks, stopping-condition records and publication preparation. The framework distinguishes between: Proposed scientific or engineering concepts Implemented reference software Functionally tested components Independently validated systems Regulated or authorized deployments Future research candidates This separation prevents conceptual completeness from being confused with demonstrated scientific, engineering, clinical or legal validity. Adversarial Materiality Fixed-Point Closure The system incorporates an adversarial closure model intended to preserve material distinctions and uncertainty. A candidate edition may reach a bounded stopping condition when its declared scope has been examined and the applicable verification requirements have been addressed. Closure remains conditional and explicitly records unresolved limitations, adverse evidence, test failures and circumstances requiring renewed investigation. Reported ongoing harm, unresolved safety concerns or materially incomplete evidence must not be automatically reclassified as verified safety or successful resolution. Universal Research and Interoperability The Future Editions System is designed as an extensible foundation for future interdisciplinary work involving mathematics, physics, biology, medicine, artificial intelligence, software and hardware engineering, robotics, energy, transportation, communications, environmental systems, disaster resilience, cybersecurity, accessibility, public services and institutional governance. It also accommodates proposed legal and international adoption architectures, including speculative applications to future interplanetary or interstellar cooperation. These application areas are research directions and design spaces, not claims of completed inventions, universally enacted laws or operational planetary-scale infrastructure. Scientific hypotheses, engineering prototypes, legal proposals, philosophical interpretations and spiritual concepts remain distinguishable according to their respective evidence and validation requirements. Human Oversight and Recoverability The framework prioritizes accountable human decision-making, reversible development, preservation of earlier versions, independent review and the protection of vulnerable people. Automated candidate generation does not constitute authorization for autonomous deployment in medical, legal, policing, military or other safety-critical environments. Implementation and deployment remain subject to the relevant scientific, technical, ethical and regulatory requirements. Included Research Artifacts This publication contains two complementary artifacts: 1. Boundary Future-Ready Consolidated PDF A 326-page consolidated document preserving the preceding research material and introducing the architecture for managing future editions, bounded closure, provenance and continued development. 2. Boundary AMFPC Future Editions System — Executable ZIP An integrated archive containing the preserved Boundary release material, an offline candidate-edition generator, machine-readable structures, integrity records, verification utilities and operating instructions. Research Contribution The principal contribution of this publication is a reproducible, provenance-aware framework for managing the transition from a bounded research artifact to successive candidate editions. It provides a structured means of preserving established work while allowing new distinctions, observations, failures, corrections and discoveries to be introduced without silently rewriting the historical record. The included mathematical enumeration and automated checks validate only their explicitly defined properties. They do not establish universal scientific completeness or independent validation of every inherited module. Conclusion Boundary — Future Editions System establishes an extensible architecture for research continuity in which finite formal analysis, recoverability, evidence preservation and future development coexist. Its governing principle is that scientific and technological progress should remain open to correction while preserving the conditions necessary for safety, accountability and continued inquiry. A finite system may reach a verified stopping condition within its declared scope. The future remains open to new evidence, new distinctions and new development.

Abstract This chapter focuses on definitions of creativity and the implications for education. This is a timely and necessary discussion because there are quite a number of definitions, and some apply better than others to education. In addition, the advent of artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how creativity is defined and how it is supported, and this means that care must be taken to ensure that the requirements for the authentic creativity of students are given priority. This chapter begins by summarizing how creativity was defined before the advent of AI (the “standard definition”). Various suggested additions and changes to the standard definition are also reviewed. These are evaluated using specific considerations, namely What should be required of a definition of creativity? What should be required of each dimension (e.g., originality) included in a definition? Are definitions parsimonious and do they avoid conflating creativity with related capacities? and Is it possible to have a definition that applies to all creativity and generalizes to all kinds of creativity and all students? The most useful definition would be externally valid and apply broadly to different groups and different kinds of creativity. The last consideration used in this chapter to evaluate definitions can also be posed as a question: Do the dimensions specified differentiate between the authentic creativity of students and the pseudo-creativity of AI? Implications for education are explored throughout this chapter and then summarized in the last section.

Fetal growth restriction (FGR) is a major obstetric complication associated with increased perinatal morbidity, mortality, and adverse long-term metabolic outcomes in adulthood. Placental dysfunction stands as the principal driver in a substantial proportion of cases, with accumulating evidence indicating that the disruption of placental redox homeostasis plays a central role in its pathophysiology. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of redox dysregulation in FGR, extending beyond classical oxidative injury to incorporate emerging non-linear paradigms. Excessive production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), coupled with inadequate antioxidant defenses, promotes lipid, protein, and DNA damage, thereby impairing trophoblast function, vascular remodeling, cell survival, and nutrient transport. Crucially, this review integrates recent breakthroughs in the fields of iron-dependent ferroptosis, endoplasmic reticulum stress, and complex redox-epigenetic cross-talk mediated by non-coding RNAs ("redox-miRs"). Furthermore, we address the translational failure of conventional systemic antioxidant therapies, highlighting the newly recognized paradox of reductive stress, where over-supplementation disrupts essential ROS-dependent signaling cascades during early placentation. To resolve these diagnostic and therapeutic limitations, this work evaluates the clinical utility of multi-omics integration for mapping placental metabolic reprogramming and artificial intelligence (AI) machine learning models that combine maternal serum redox biomarkers with longitudinal fetal Doppler metrics for early risk stratification. Finally, we explore next-generation obstetric frontiers, including placenta-targeted nanomedicine for localized drug delivery, Placenta-on-a-Chip microfluidic and organoid screening platforms, and autologous mitochondrial transplantation aimed at rescuing syncytiotrophoblast bioenergetics. Overall, current evidence underscores placental redox dysregulation as an interconnected, systemic failure rather than an isolated molecular defect. Moving toward precision, redox-guided perinatal management requires longitudinal human studies and well-designed clinical trials to validate whether the targeted restoration of redox homeostasis can translate into improved maternal, fetal, and neonatal outcomes.

Clinical investigations of high-risk medical devices generate essential evidence for regulatory decisions concerning implanted, life-supporting, and potentially harmful devices. Traditional monitoring approaches, characterized by frequent on-site visits and extensive source data verification (SDV), are resource-intensive and may provide limited additional value in detecting critical errors. Risk-based monitoring (RBM), supported by risk-based quality management (RBQM), focuses monitoring activities on processes and data essential for participant safety and trial reliability. International regulatory bodies, including the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH), US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), European Medicines Agency (EMA), and International Organization for Standardization (ISO), support risk-proportionate quality management. In India, clinical investigations are governed by the Medical Devices Rules, 2017, administered by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO); however, dedicated provisions for RBM remain limited. This review examines global and Indian regulatory approaches to RBM in Class C and D medical device investigations. It discusses key components, including risk assessment, key risk indicators, quality tolerance limits, centralized monitoring, and targeted source data review. Published evidence regarding effectiveness, costs, and operational benefits is evaluated alongside device-specific challenges, implementation barriers, and emerging technologies such as electronic data capture, artificial intelligence, wearable sensors, and decentralized clinical trials. Traditional and risk-based monitoring approaches are compared, and a roadmap for integrating RBM into India's regulatory framework is proposed. RBM represents a scientifically justified and regulatorily supportable approach for high-risk medical device investigations, provided that a device-specific, CDSCO-aligned framework ensures documented risk assessment, proportionate monitoring, participant protection, data integrity, and auditable oversight.

This research proposal outlines an exploratory study into how employability expectations and the growing integration of programming, computational tools, simulation environments, and generative artificial intelligence may be reshaping students’ understandings of engineering knowledge and technical competence. It proposes to examine how engineering students perceive the relationship between programming proficiency, theoretical understanding, practical experimentation, and discipline-specific skills, particularly as software-based work becomes increasingly prominent in education and professional practice. The proposal also considers how these changing perceptions may influence group dynamics, expectations of competence, divisions of responsibility, recognition of contributions, and experiences of perceived inequity or dissatisfaction in collaborative settings. Drawing on Expectation States Theory and perspectives on equity, the proposed study adopts an exploratory qualitative approach to investigate how students interpret and experience these changes in the meaning and valuation of engineering competence.

Writing correct access control policies for software applications is difficult because it requires expertise in the authorization language and a thorough understanding of the application's authorization requirements. Existing synthesis and mining approaches assume explicit authorization inputs and a trusted reference policy. However, authorization logic is often distributed across code, comments, and documentation rather than captured in a single artifact, and developer-defined policies in real-world application repositories are often incomplete, outdated, or incorrect. We present Reparo, an LLM-aided pipeline for access control policy synthesis, repair, and validation. Reparo collects repository evidence for authorization intent and uses it to guide an LLM in generating an initial policy. It then uses official policy-language validation tools to identify and automatically repair errors. For semantic validation, a different LLM derives a behavioral oracle from the same repository evidence, consisting of concrete authorization requests with expected allow or deny decisions, which Reparo executes against the generated policy. We manually assess the oracle on a statistically sized sample of 390 test cases. We evaluate Reparo on 228 real-world GitHub repositories that use Cedar, OpenFGA, or Rego. In these repositories, 40.6-55.7% of the repository policies fail their language's validation tool, whereas Reparo produces 99.0-100% valid policies after repair. Agreement with the oracle is 98.2-99.6% for OpenFGA, 82.0-86.5% for Cedar, and 76.3-80.2% for Rego. Manual review confirms 91.5-96.9% of the sampled test cases as correct. Synthesizing and validating the policy for one repository takes about five minutes and costs $0.55-$1.57. These results show that repository evidence can support both access policy synthesis and independent validation, even when no reliable reference policy exists.

Reproducing deep learning (DL) bugs is challenging because failures can involve source code, models, data, dependencies, and execution environments. Incomplete bug reports further complicate reproduction by omitting essential details. We present RepGen, an open-source tool for reproducing DL bugs through context-aware code generation and iterative verification. Given a bug report and repository, RepGen explores the codebase to build a learning-enhanced context, develop a reproduction plan, and generate candidate scripts. It refines candidates using static checks and LLM feedback to improve their correctness and relevance. When enabled, the tool prepares the execution environment, runs the script, and assesses its output against the reported failure. RepGen provides an interactive command-line interface supporting local and hosted LLMs, configurable execution budgets, and inspectable artifacts, along with a GitHub Action for automated issue processing. The underlying approach reproduced 85 of 106 real-world DL bugs (80.19%). A controlled study with 27 developers showed a 23.35% improvement in reproduction success and a 56.8% reduction in reproduction time.

A significant milestone in the field of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), particularly large language models (LLMs), was reached with the introduction of the ChatGPT system by OpenAI in late 2022. Subsequently, other advanced models like Anthropic’s Claude and Google’s Gemini were released, broadening the possibilities for meaningful human–machine conversations (Hu, 2023). These systems, utilizing advanced natural language processing technologies, exhibit remarkable capabilities in managing dialogue, grasping context, and generating high-quality content. Creative AI has rapidly become integrated into the organizational and practical aspects of social work, and GenAI is already widely utilized by professionals and students (Singer et al., 2023; Tulğan & Güre, 2024). The question confronting social work educators is no longer whether to involve AI, but rather how to do so effectively to prepare students for critical, ethical, and proficient practice. Addressing this issue entails more than merely incorporating AI content into existing courses. It necessitates a learning environment that transforms the student’s interaction with GenAI from that of a passive user to that of an informed professional, someone capable of assessing a GenAI tool based on the specific requirements of a practice scenario, recognizing its limitations, and making well-founded decisions on when and how to use it. Social work students also need to know how to create AI-based tools for everyday practice (Kapur et al., 2025; Reamer, 2023; Stone, 2023; Tulğan & Güre, 2024). These advancements call for adapting social work education and learning methodologies to the digital era while incorporating advanced LLMs into professional teaching and training processes (Kapur et al., 2025; Singer et al., 2023).
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Digital transformation has intensified questions about the sustainability of educational systems, yet sustainable digital education is often discussed in terms of technological capacity, access, efficiency and scalability. This conceptual article develops a distinct conceptualisation of responsive digital pedagogy (RDP) for the social sustainability of digital education. Drawing on scholarship on social sustainability, digital education, relational pedagogy, student agency and sociotechnical educational infrastructures, and informed by peer-reviewed research on responsive and democratic pedagogies, the article distinguishes sustainable educational provision from sustainable educational experience. It proposes four interconnected dimensions: relational sustainability, concerning recognition and pedagogical response; temporal sustainability, concerning attention and differentiated rhythms; participatory sustainability, concerning agency, plurality and meaningful influence; and infrastructural sustainability, concerning the technological and institutional conditions that organise educational possibility. These dimensions are examined through tensions between efficiency and attention, visibility and meaningful participation, scalability and relational density, and predictability and pedagogical openness. Socially sustainable digital education is therefore defined as the capacity of a digitally mediated educational ecology to maintain over time the relational, temporal, participatory and infrastructural conditions through which meaningful educational participation remains possible. The framework is presented as an analytical proposition for further empirical refinement rather than as a validated measurement model.

Self-supervised learning relies on asymmetry between what a model observes and what it must explain. Recent methods learn 3D geometry from unposed images by predicting cameras and scene structure, then rendering held-out views. To avoid trivial solutions, they impose this asymmetry in the input space, restricting how views interact through separate branches or masked attention. We revisit this design with geometric accuracy, rather than rendering quality, as the main objective. When a held-out view lies between context views, the context already constrains the geometry it observes. We therefore impose the asymmetry in the 3D representation space, excluding held-out views only from the reconstructed scene while a shared backbone uses all views for correspondence. This improves depth and pose estimation over input-space designs. We further exploit view density: sparse and dense observations depict the same scene but provide different amounts of correspondence. Aligning sparse-context features with dense-context features supplies a geometric training signal alongside rendering, without a pretrained geometric teacher. We additionally align features with a frozen vision foundation model, which brings further gains. None of these signals requires geometric annotation, and the resulting model improves geometry estimation over prior self-supervised methods. Controlled experiments isolate the contribution of each component, and self-supervised pretraining also improves subsequent supervised training.

Abstract AI models have enabled substantial advances in health care. Since the entry into force of the European Union (EU) AI Act in 2024, these systems have become subject to a common regulatory framework in the EU intended to harmonize AI governance across all member states. One of the act’s distinctive features is that it accommodates existing economic, technological, and regulatory differences among European countries by leaving certain implementation responsibilities to national authorities. This is evident in regulatory sandboxes, supervised environments for developing, testing, and validating AI systems before deployment. In this viewpoint, we provide a policy-oriented analysis of health care regulatory sandboxes under the EU AI Act and propose recommendations for their design. These recommendations address the need to document model compression techniques that may affect the classification of large high-risk systems above the 10 25 floating point operations per second threshold, incorporate explainability into AI systems from the design stage, identify and document biases in health care datasets, clarify the treatment of federated learning parameter updates under the General Data Protection Regulation, and strengthen the oversight of AI agents in clinical environments. The implementation timeline makes this discussion particularly timely given the approaching deadline of August 2, 2027, by which all member states must have established at least one national regulatory sandbox.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) recognizes the negative health impact of occupational exposure to anesthetic gases in the operating room. As a result, OSHA has implemented regulations, engineering controls, and regular air quality surveillance programs to protect surgical staff. However, immediate postoperative patients exhale waste anesthetic gases (WAGs) into the Post Anesthesia Care Unit (PACU) environment, exposing nurses to occupational health risks, including headaches, fatigue, organ damage, cancer, and reproductive complications. The PACU lacks any regulations or even recognition of this safety issue; in fact, most nurses and leadership are unaware. One potential solution, a scavenging oxygen mask system used on these patients, captures WAGs while delivering oxygen and protecting nurses. This mask was tested at a community surgery center and was then permanently implemented as a standard. Additional testing of the scavenging oxygen mask system at Purdue University a few years later revealed the mask also removed over 94% of microbes/pathogens from patients’ exhaled breath. This additional health benefit could also protect PACU nurses from patients’ expired respiratory infectious particles, as it is common practice in the PACU for patients to cough and breathe deeply to enhance their recovery. To test this potential benefit, this PACU examined the scavenging mask’s effect on nurses’ infectious illness as measured by nurse absenteeism. Methods A retrospective analysis of nurse callouts and absenteeism for infectious illnesses or WAGs exposure symptoms was completed comparing 4 years preimplementation and 3 years postimplementation of the scavenging masks at a single hospital-based PACU. Results The surgery center experienced significantly reduced PACU nurse callouts due to infectious illnesses by approximately 60% (P = .034) after the implementation of the scavenging mask system. Conclusion This research highlights the dual benefit of WAG removal and respiratory infection control, supporting the scavenging mask’s effectiveness in safeguarding health care workers (HCWs).

documents.abstract: Large language models offer a promising route to register-transfer-level (RTL) design, but reliable implementations require checking and revision based on electronic design automation (EDA) tools' feedback. Existing RTL-specialized models often lack learned interaction with such EDA tools or rely on separate generation and repair components. We introduce RTL-Interact, a multi-task post-training framework that trains a single RTL-specialized model to generate RTL, construct task-appropriate EDA checks, and revise implementations using tool feedback. The framework combines automatically constructed multi-task demonstrations with staged supervision from chain-of-thought to tool-integrated reasoning. We further introduce Pattern-Aware Policy Optimization (PAPO) for multi-task reinforcement learning. PAPO augments Group Relative Policy Optimization with correctness-gated rewards that favor concise successful checking while rewarding effective revision, and uses task grouping to preserve coverage across objectives. On CVDP, RTL-Interact-32B achieves 48.7% weighted Pass@1 and 68.9% Pass@5, surpassing its teacher model, DeepSeek-V3.2, while RTL-Interact-8B achieves 44.9% weighted Pass@1. Additionally, we show that PAPO can reduce average tool calls by 63.8% while improving Pass@1. Both models also outperform all RTL-specialized baselines on VerilogEval v2 and RTLLM v2, demonstrating the effectiveness of our method.

Abstract The 28 March 2025 Mw 7.7 Myanmar earthquake showed that a large regional earthquake can produce extensive ground shaking throughout Thailand even though it occurred 1000 km away. This earthquake caused prolonged shaking of high-rise buildings and disruption of activities in major cities, emphasizing the need for rapid earthquake information to support community response. Although Thailand maintains national seismic monitoring networks, there has been no operational earthquake early warning (EEW) available to the public. This article presents RUGON (Real-time Ubiquitous Ground-shaking Observation Network), a community-based earthquake observation and rapid response platform designed to deliver timely ground-motion information by integrating distributed microelectromechanical systems accelerometers, edge computing, cloud processing, and web-based decision-support tools. The platform supports community notification, structural vibration monitoring, and real-time situational awareness during earthquake emergencies. Analysis of strong-motion records from the 28 March 2025 Myanmar earthquake shows that, if rapid detection and communication are implemented, a regional earthquake may provide more than one minute of available lead time for major Thai cities. Sensor performance was verified through laboratory calibration against laser Doppler vibrometer measurements. Field deployment during the 18 May 2026 ML 5.3 Myanmar earthquake successfully demonstrated the complete RUGON workflow, from sensing and communication to notification and visualization, under real earthquake conditions. RUGON is a rapid earthquake information and situational-awareness platform that reports observed ground motion in near-real time for rapid alert and response. It is not a substitute for a national EEW system. Nevertheless, because regional earthquakes affecting Thailand originate from distant sources, even peak-ground-acceleration-based observations without P-wave prediction still provide a usable interval for alert and response. Community-scale observations of strong shaking upstream can provide actionable information before it reaches distant communities.

European rural communities face profound transformations driven by demographic change, economic restructuring, service erosion, and political marginalisation. In response, Rural Movements (RMs) and Rural Parliaments (RPs) have emerged as important actors shaping the socio-political dimensions of rural landscapes. Drawing on the European Landscape Convention’s understanding of landscape as shaped by both natural and human factors, this article conceptualises RMs and RPs as co-producers of rural socio-political landscapes through advocacy, identity-building, community mobilisation, and institutional engagement. The study combines a qualitative literature review with exploratory empirical material from two expert workshops conducted at the 6th European Rural Parliament (Inverurie, Scotland, October 2025), involving representatives from eight European countries. The analysis examines RMs and RPs as agents of social innovation, arenas of identity preservation and reinvention, infrastructures of democratic renewal, and navigators of the professionalisation-institutionalisation dilemma. Findings suggest that many movements emerged in response to centralisation, service loss, weakened local influence, and democratic deficits. Professionalisation is understood as the development of organisational capacities, advocacy skills, and strategic networks while maintaining grassroots legitimacy and local embeddedness. The article identifies key factors that enable and constrain movement development and concludes that the transformative potential of RMs and RPs depends on balancing organisational effectiveness with participatory, locally rooted, and politically autonomous forms of action.

Background Large language models (LLMs) may support patient education, but their suitability for diabetic kidney disease (DKD) remains uncertain. We compared six publicly accessible LLM chatbots—ChatGPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, Doubao, Kimi, and Qwen—across safety, accuracy, empathy, information quality, and readability, with safety as the primary outcome. Methods In this CHART-guided cross-sectional study, 42 standardized English DKD questions were submitted once to each chatbot in independent single-turn sessions, generating 252 responses. Five source-masked clinical raters assessed safety, accuracy, empathy, DISCERN, EQIP, JAMA benchmarks, and the Global Quality Scale; readability was assessed automatically. Agreement was evaluated using Fleiss' κ and ICC (2,1)/ICC (2,5). Model differences were tested using Cochran's Q or Friedman tests with Kendall's W and Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Potentially unsafe responses underwent qualitative review. Results Safety showed substantial agreement ( κ = 0.854); ICC (2,1) ranged from 0.552 to 0.855 and ICC (2,5) from 0.860 to 0.967. Safe-response rates ranged from 83.3% to 92.9% without significant between-model differences ( P = 0.726). Accuracy and empathy differed significantly (both P < 0.001), with ChatGPT highest for accuracy and Gemini highest for clinician-rated empathy. Information quality also differed significantly, with ChatGPT performing best overall and Doubao lowest. All six readability indices differed across models (all P < 0.001; Kendall's W = 0.139–0.255). DeepSeek had the lowest mean scores on all five grade-level indices and the highest mean FRES, but mean grade-level estimates exceeded the sixth-grade reference level for every model. Thirty of 252 responses (11.9%) were potentially unsafe, most often because of incomplete medication-related information or insufficiently individualized fluid advice. Conclusions Publicly accessible LLMs can provide plausible DKD information but show variable performance and safety risks. They may support, but should not replace, professional patient education; guideline anchoring, source verification, improved readability, and clinical oversight remain essential.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The continuous deployment of enterprise voice systems creates a critical operational bottleneck: evaluating the acoustic quality of synthetic speech across high-volume production updates. While human Mean Opinion Score (MOS) remains the quality gold standard, it introduces severe operational costs and turn-around delays that make continuous integration infeasible. In this work, we present a system design case study for a scalable, low-cost and offline evaluation pipeline capable of scoring large batches of synthetic speech at marginal cost. First, we use Qwen2-Audio-7B-Instruct in a zero-shot setting for granular MOS estimation, noticing perceptual blind spots and inherent biases. Then, we analyze SOMOS dataset and construct a diagnostic benchmark that operationalizes two prosodic dimensions associated with human naturalness ratings. Finally, we adapt Qwen2-Audio-7B-Instruct through a parameter-efficient finetuning (LoRA) on the task of MOS evaluation, observing improvements over base model and widely used neural baselines like UTMOS and establishing a practical blueprint for enterprise-grade speech quality assurance.

Recent advances in single-cell technologies have enabled the profiling of multiple molecular modalities, including transcriptomics, proteomics, and chromatin accessibility, providing a more comprehensive understanding of cellular states. However, integrating heterogeneous modalities and predicting missing molecular information remain challenging, particularly when paired measurements are limited. Here, we introduce scAnyOmics, a generative framework that distills knowledge from a frozen single-cell foundation model into a multimodal student model. scAnyOmics integrates scRNA-seq, protein-marker measurements, and scATAC-seq into a shared representation, enabling cross-modal prediction and reconstruction of missing modalities. We assembled 690,880 cells from six publicly available studies, covering both paired and partially paired multi-omics measurements, to systematically evaluate its predictive performance. We further evaluated scAnyOmics on held-out donor data, where it outperformed baseline methods across multiple evaluation metrics. Beyond cross-modal reconstruction, we explored its applications in cell-type annotation, perturbation-response prediction, and biological age estimation. Overall, scAnyOmics provides a unified framework for integrating incomplete single-cell multi-omics data and transferring pretrained biological knowledge, supporting the development of virtual cell models across diverse cellular contexts and experimental platforms.

This technical note examines proof steps in ‘The Schur complement inequalities involving sectorial matrices’ by Marziyeh Irandegani, Mojtaba Bakherad and Monire Hajmohamadi (Linear and Multilinear Algebra, 2026; DOI: 10.1080/03081087.2026.2751934). An exact positive-definite 2×2 example disproves the interchange of a Schur complement with an integral used in the proofs of Theorems 2.2, 2.6 and 2.9. A separate sectorial example disproves an intermediate norm comparison in the proof of Proposition 3.1. These examples do not disprove the stated main inequalities. A self-contained corrected argument establishes the sharp factor sec²(α) for the matrix-mean inequality and the normalized operator-monotone functional inequality, improving the factors sec⁴(α) stated in the reviewed article. Sharpness is established for every fixed positive block size. A unitarily invariant norm consequence has factor sec³(α), improving sec⁵(α); optimality of the norm factor is not claimed. The final conclusion of the reviewed Proposition 3.1 is explicitly left unresolved. No exhaustive literature-priority claim is made. Files: the technical note in PDF and a ZIP package containing the PDF, editable LaTeX source, README and a Python script using exact rational arithmetic to verify the displayed examples. The reviewed publisher PDF is not redistributed. AI assistance and author responsibility: OpenAI ChatGPT was used for English-language improvement, computational checks and auxiliary mathematical analysis, including assistance with derivations and counterexample verification. The author takes full responsibility for the construction and validity of the counterexamples, the statements of the lemmas and theorems, all proofs, and the final content of this note.

Generative AI has become a common source of health information for Chinese university students. While existing research has examined trust and adoption intention toward AI-generated health information, two gaps remain. First, the dominant risk assumed in the literature is explicit factual error (hallucination); far less attention has been paid to "implicit misinformation" — content that is fluent and professional-looking but misleading through hedged/vague wording (e.g., "may pose a risk to some groups") or evidence overclaiming (e.g., generalizing animal or small-sample findings to humans). Second, AI-labeling regulations are being rolled out in China, but it is unknown whether an "AI-generated" label helps or hinders users in detecting problematic content. The label may act as a warning cue for explicit errors, yet function as a quality guarantee ("AI is cautious in wording") for implicit misleads, reducing vigilance. A 2 (AI-generated label: present vs. absent) × 2 (content: implicitly misleading vs. accurate control) between-subjects online experiment among Chinese university students aged 18–26. Target sample: N = 320 (80 per cell). Study author: Huang Yuanjing, Department of Journalism and Communication, Peking University. Status: Registration draft in preparation; not yet submitted as a formal preregistration.

The rapid expansion of large scale computer networks driven by cloud infrastructures, Internet of Things environments, and distributed digital services has significantly increased the complexity of cybersecurity threats. Traditional rule based security systems often struggle to detect evolving and previously unseen attacks within high volume network traffic. This study proposes a self learning artificial intelligence approach designed to enhance threat detection capability in large scale computer networks by leveraging adaptive learning mechanisms and large scale network data analysis. The proposed framework integrates machine learning models with big data processing techniques to continuously learn from network traffic patterns, behavioral anomalies, and historical security events. Through automated feature extraction and iterative model refinement, the system dynamically improves its ability to identify malicious activities without relying solely on predefined signatures. This study adopts a qualitative conceptual evaluation approach to examine the proposed self-learning artificial intelligence and big data framework for cybersecurity resilience in distributed computer networks. The evaluation is conducted through literature synthesis, comparative analysis of existing intrusion detection approaches, architectural modeling, and conceptual validation of the proposed framework against key cybersecurity requirements, including adaptability, scalability, continuous learning, and detection coverage for known and unknown threats. The system also shows strong scalability in processing high volume network data while maintaining stable detection performance. These results indicate that integrating self learning artificial intelligence with scalable data processing can strengthen cybersecurity resilience in large scale computer networks and support the development of more adaptive and intelligent network defense mechanisms for future digital infrastructures.

The rapid expansion of large-scale computer networks and the exponential growth of big data have significantly increased the complexity and frequency of cyber threats, rendering traditional signature-based security mechanisms inadequate for adaptive detection. This study aims to develop a self-learning AI model capable of autonomously identifying evolving attack patterns and anomalous behaviors in large-scale networks without relying exclusively on pre-labeled datasets. The proposed framework integrates deep neural architectures, incremental learning, and behavior-based traffic analysis to enable continuous adaptation to dynamic threat environments while ensuring computational efficiency and scalability. The model was trained and evaluated using realistic network traffic datasets simulating distributed attacks, zero-day exploits, and advanced persistent threats across heterogeneous environments. Experimental findings demonstrate that the self-learning approach enhances detection accuracy, reduces false positives, and accelerates response times compared to conventional intrusion detection systems. In addition, the combination of deep neural architectures with incremental learning and scalable data processing further strengthens model robustness and adaptability in complex and evolving networks. The results indicate that integrating adaptive AI into cybersecurity frameworks enhances proactive defense capabilities, improves resilience in large-scale computer networks, and provides a scalable, intelligent solution for next-generation threat detection systems. This study highlights the practical relevance of combining AI, big data analytics, and cybersecurity strategies to support intelligent, adaptive security solutions capable of addressing emerging threats, minimizing operational risks, and fostering robust network protection in increasingly complex digital infrastructures.
topics: Internet Traffic Analysis and Secure E-voting

documents.abstract: Representing 3D shapes using a set of primitives - known as shape abstraction - is an actively studied problem in computer graphics with wide applications in shape understanding, analysis, and simulation due to the compactness and computational efficiency of the primitive-based representation. Prior work has primarily focused on geometry-aware shape abstraction, where the objective is to approximate the input shape with a minimal set of primitives while preserving geometric fidelity. However, these methods often overlook semantic consistency, inevitably leading to primitives that span across multiple semantic parts. Such inconsistency can cause undesirable artifacts in downstream tasks such as part-level shape editing or manipulation. In this paper, we introduce a new task - semantic-aware shape abstraction, where the goal is to produce abstractions that are both geometrically faithful and semantically consistent, ensuring that each primitive adheres strictly to a single semantic part without crossing semantic boundaries. We propose SemEllipsoid, a novel method to address this problem using ellipsoidal primitives. The core idea is to inject semantic constraints into the primitive optimization process leveraging the availability of semantic cues from large-scale foundation models. We design a fully differentiable projection-blending-evaluation scheme to measure semantic divergence against input semantic masks, and formulate an alternating optimization strategy to iteratively solve for optimal semantic assignment and primitive configurations. Our method is non-learning-based, requiring no data collection or network training, and generalizes well to shapes from arbitrary categories. It also supports different levels of abstraction according to user demand. Extensive experiments and evaluations validate the effectiveness of our approach across several 3D shape collections.

Written companion to the guest lecture "Seven Human Qualities for the New Era: Leadership Beyond Artificial Intelligence", delivered by Prof. Dr. Stoyana Natseva as a pre-recorded lecture at the international webinar "Your Future Starts Now: Leadership and Innovation for Finance and Business", organised by Kimyo International University in Tashkent (KIUT), Uzbekistan, on 14 October 2026. The paper is not a transcript; it sets out the argument of the lecture in academic form. Starting from the observation that people often know what they should do and still find it difficult to do it, the paper proposes seven human qualities that may matter more as artificial intelligence makes information widely available: emotional maturity, adaptability, the ability to learn, critical thinking, responsibility, resilience, and the ability to communicate and work with people. Each quality is related to established research and to its implications for finance and business education. The seven qualities are presented as a teaching framework for discussion, not as a validated competency model. This version has not undergone peer review.

This study examines how digital leadership shapes public employees’ perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI), with innovation climate modeled as a mediating mechanism under Social Learning Theory. Survey data from 314 public employees in southern Türkiye were analyzed using structural equation modeling. Results indicate that digital leadership positively predicts both innovation climate and AI perceptions, and that innovation climate itself enhances AI perceptions. Mediation analysis shows a partial indirect effect of digital leadership on AI perceptions through innovation climate. The study links leadership and organizational climate perspectives to explain technology-related perceptions in the public sector and suggests that strengthening digital leadership capabilities and cultivating an innovation-oriented climate are critical for effective and sustainable AI adoption in public administration.

This article reflects on the process, challenges and outcomes of a pilot project that explored the use of a participatory, game-based approach to developing children's critical capabilities with respect to AI literacy. The pilot focused on AI sycophancy: the tendency of Large Language Models (LLMs) to flatter and agree with users, prioritising likability and ongoing engagement over accuracy. Our multidisciplinary team combined expertise in communication and media studies, technology regulation, machine learning, and early childhood education, and actively involved children at various points in the process. We designed a bespoke 'explainer' animation and an interactive 'game' based on custom-built voice chatbots, which we delivered in a workshop with children aged 6-10. The article discusses the process of developing and delivering the pilot, navigating disciplinary boundaries, children's responses to the experience, and the trade-offs involved in a participatory approach to AI ethics for children.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The evaluation of new medical concepts and digital health devices for rare diseases is hampered by the scarcity and vulnerability of real-world patient cohorts.Synthetic sampling (Silicon Sampling) using personas driven by large language models (LLMs) offers a promising digital evaluation framework, but one that is biased by 'algorithmic perfection': over-rational decision-making, omniscience via retrieval-from-sources (RAG) and sycophancy.This article establishes a methodological framework based on the meta-ergonomics of falsification and the Adversarial Cognitive Twin (ACT) architecture.Rather than increasing the persona's theoretical intelligence, we propose to falsify the synthetic agent by injecting it with calibrated cognitive impairments, semantic entropy, reduced user knowledge bases and multiagent contradiction loops.This methodological constraint enables the simulation of mental load, doubts and user resistance -characteristics specific to clinical reality.An experimental benchmarking protocol based on secondary data enables the measurement of error alignment and the rate of compliance inhibition.This work defines a robust and ethical framework for use, compliant with the requirements of the EU AI Act, positioning the constrained persona as a filter for user resistance prior to in vivo clinical research.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Synergy of Human Capital 5.0 and Artificial Intelligence in Business Decision-Making to Enhance MSME Competitiveness in the Digital Economy Era. The digital economy and the spread of artificial intelligence (AI) and automation are changing how micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) make decisions and which skills they need. However, AI adoption does not automatically improve competitiveness because it depends on the readiness of people and management. This article aims to (1) analyze how AI disruption and automation reshape competence requirements in MSMEs, (2) examine the role of Human Capital 5.0 in using AI for business decisions, (3) identify opportunities, challenges, and the roles of management and education in human–AI synergy, and (4) formulate a conceptual framework of that synergy. The study is a structured qualitative literature review of 29 sources published in 2022–2026, consisting of international and national journal articles, the author’s earlier studies, and reports from international and government institutions, analyzed through thematic synthesis. The review shows that the literature mostly addresses AI adoption from technological and organizational angles, while human competence as a determinant of decision quality has not been fully integrated. Human Capital 5.0 functions as the ability to interpret, test, and control AI outputs, whereas AI extends data-processing and prediction capacity. Management shapes this synergy through leadership, human resource development, and responsible AI governance, while education supplies competencies and collaboration with MSMEs. The article proposes a five-stage conceptual model supported by leadership, digital readiness, data quality, technology access, and ethics, together with four propositions for future empirical testing. The model remains propositional and requires empirical validation. Strengthening MSMEs therefore requires combining AI literacy training, mentoring, cross-sector collaboration, and responsible AI governance.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Existing sketch generation methods often rely on image guidance and are largely limited to individual objects or simplified scenes, leaving text-guided complex scene sketching underexplored. We present SketchDirector, an agentic framework that mimics the human sketching workflow for automatic multi-concept scene sketching. Given a scene-level text prompt, SketchDirector first employs a large language model~(LLM) to decompose the scene into multiple draft assets, where each is represented by a set of Bézier curves. Then, an agentic reasoning loop iteratively plans and executes their spatial arrangement, guided by self-evolving memory. Finally, a detail refinement module leverages diffusion priors to enhance sketch quality while preserving geometric structure. To support future research and applications in multi-concept scene sketch generation, we further introduce the \textit{MCSketch8K} dataset, comprising editable vector assets, compositional layouts, and object-level manipulation annotations. Extensive experiments show that SketchDirector outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in semantic and compositional quality while effectively preserving overall contour organization during refinement. The project page is: \href{https://yiki77.github.io/SketchDirector/}{https://yiki77.github.io/SketchDirector/}.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

documents.abstract: Runway surface conditions, particularly in cold and icy environments, pose a significant challenge to aircraft operations. To enhance safety and standardisation, the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) introduced the Global Reporting Format (GRF) in 2021, replacing previous assessment methods, including SNOWTAM reports and braking action conditions. This study critically evaluates the implementation of the GRF, analysing its impact on two key aviation stakeholders: airport operators and flight crews. It also includes a comprehensive literature review on the evolution of runway condition reporting since 1956.The research incorporates an extensive survey and comparative analysis, summarising the opinions and feedback of both pilots and airport operators. While pilots largely appreciate the improved clarity and structure of the updated SNOWTAM format, concerns remain over the removal of braking action assessments, which previously aided aircraft performance calculations and improved the situational awareness. Additionally, the study highlights inconsistencies across different airports, particularly in the measurement of runway contaminants. Airport operators have expressed concerns about the subjectivity of visual assessments, the absence of standardised measurement techniques, and the limitations of the Runway Condition Assessment Matrix (RCAM), which does not account for different runway surfaces.The findings suggest that while the GRF has improved global standardisation and efficiency in runway condition reporting, further refinements are necessary to enhance consistency and reliability. The study proposes measures to address current limitations, including improved contaminant measurement techniques and a reassessment of the methodology to incorporate variations in runway surface properties. These insights contribute to the ongoing discourse on aviation safety and provide recommendations for optimising runway surface condition reporting, particularly in cold weather environments.

Rapid urbanization in Southeast Asia has created complex, heterogeneous landscapes that facilitate the proliferation of Aedes mosquitoes, the primary vectors of dengue, chikungunya, Zika, and other arboviruses. Megacities present particular surveillance challenges because vector populations vary across neighborhoods, building types, microhabitats, and vertical levels, while conventional indices may provide incomplete information on adult abundance and transmission risk. This narrative review synthesizes conventional and emerging approaches for monitoring immature and adult Aedes mosquitoes in urban environments, with emphasis on how surveillance tools can be combined to answer operational public-health questions. We examine the strengths, limitations, operational requirements, and urban applicability of larval surveys, ovitraps, adult traps, automated monitoring, molecular approaches, remote sensing, community-based surveillance, and artificial-intelligence-enabled systems. Rather than treating individual tools as interchangeable, we consider surveillance design across horizontal and vertical urban strata and discuss how sampling intensity can be adapted to local heterogeneity, resource availability, and the decision that surveillance is intended to support. We further examine how entomological observations can be integrated with epidemiological data, weather, land use, urban morphology, and human mobility to identify areas requiring intensified investigation or control. The review proposes a decision-oriented and tiered framework in which low-cost or automated sentinel surveillance provides continuous situational awareness, while targeted field investigation is triggered by entomological, environmental, epidemiological, or model-based signals. This perspective provides practical guidance for developing scalable, context-appropriate surveillance systems for rapidly urbanizing Southeast Asian cities.

Facility location problems (FLPs) underpin decisions in emergency response, healthcare access, and infrastructure siting, yet applying them requires both optimization modeling skills and substantial spatial data preparation. This paper presents SOCA (Spatial Optimization Conversational Agent), a system that confines a large language model (LLM) to classifying the formulation and extracting scalar parameters through schema-validated function calls and delegates study area resolution, open-data acquisition, distance computation, and exact solution of four classic FLP formulations (P-Median, P-Center, MCLP, and LSCP) to deterministic tools. Every specification is confirmed by the user before solving, and solutions can be reported with substitutability and spatial equity diagnostics. We present SOCA as a technical feasibility study. Worked examples show how requests become staged, user-confirmed specifications; the MILP encodings reproduce the optima of a reference implementation exactly; and the data pipeline returned the targeted input layers across seven study areas, including cities in Africa and South Asia, using primary or fallback sources; retrieval does not establish data quality. A Manhattan fire station case illustrates coverage trade-offs and post-solve diagnostics on road network distances. Measuring interpretation accuracy, comparison against other LLM tool workflows, and a usability study with non-technical users remain future work.

This chapter examines the social and organizational challenges involved in setting up a new industrial works, drawing on Eric J. Miller’s analysis of the Spencer Works steel plant developed by Richard Thomas & Baldwins. Miller argues that technological development routinely outpaces the evolution of social institutions, leading to underutilization of human capacity, organizational conflict, and performance gaps. Addressing these issues requires treating organization building as a central task rather than a secondary consequence of plant design. Using a socio-technical systems framework, the chapter distinguishes four interdependent tasks in establishing a new works: plant design, plant construction, organization design, and organization building. Miller demonstrates that these processes form a single system of activities whose coordination is critical to the effectiveness of the final operating organization. The Spencer Works case illustrates the risks of separating technical and organizational planning, particularly when conventional management assumptions constrain innovation in work design and authority relations. Miller highlights the paradox of expecting a future operating organization to design itself while simultaneously being shaped by inherited structures and time pressures. Subsequent integration of plant and organizational design under operational leadership allowed some anticipatory accommodation between social and technical demands, though financial, temporal, and technological constraints limited its scope. The chapter concludes that while socio-technical analysis cannot eliminate uncertainty in green-field developments, it provides a disciplined way of anticipating tensions, managing human factors, and supporting more adaptive and effective organizational formation.

The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed educational research, creating new opportunities for designing inclusive, personalized, and learner-centred educational environments. Among emerging technologies, social robotics has gained increasing attention for its potential to support the cognitive, communicative, and socio-emotional development of learners with diverse educational needs. Unlike conventional educational technologies, social robots interact naturally through speech, gestures, facial expressions, eye contact, and emotional feedback, fostering communication and active engagement (Pennazio, 2017). Digital innovation has become a strategic resource for promoting educational quality and inclusion. As Calvani (2013) argues, technology should not be viewed as an educational goal but as a pedagogical tool capable of improving learning when integrated into evidence-based teaching practices. Within this perspective, social robotics combines artificial intelligence with inclusive pedagogy, promoting participation, individualized instruction, and socio-emotional development.
